sources.note: Read through a summarizing fetch on 2026-11-17. Quoted: 'a standard index build locks out writes (but not reads) on the table until it's done'; with CONCURRENTLY 'PostgreSQL will build the index without taking any locks that prevent concurrent inserts, updates, or deletes', it 'takes significantly longer', 'CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY cannot' run in a transaction block, and a failure leaves an INVALID index. Cloud SQL Query Insights and the pg_stat_statements output are the author's scenario (Query Insights' features to verify against the Cloud SQL documentation).

brief.situation: You are the database engineer at Fennick Outdoor. This morning's release added a 'your recent orders' panel to the account page; it queries orders by customer_id, ordered by created_at. Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL orders-db is at 92% CPU and account pages take six seconds. A marketing email to two million customers goes out at 10:30, linking to the account page.
handover: orders has 80 million rows and takes about 300 writes a second from checkout.
The release cannot be rolled back without also removing a payment fix that shipped with it.
howItWorks: The terminal shows each command's output; the diagram shows the new query, the orders table and its indexes, and checkout's writes.
Each command takes a minute or two; the clock moves only when you act or wait.
When you close, you write the record and explain your reasoning.

cic.label: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY orders_customer_created_idx ON orders (customer_id, created_at DESC)
cic.available: not busy and (not fixed and not harmed)
cic.why: Already done, or the system is down.

effects.output:
dbeng@cloudshell:~$ psql -c "CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY orders_customer_created_idx ON orders (customer_id, created_at DESC)"
CREATE INDEX   (25 min; checkout writes continued throughout)

effects.log: The index matches the query's filter and order; built concurrently, it does not lock out checkout's writes. When it is valid, the query reads ten rows instead of millions.

parts.label: Why
parts.modelAnswer: Query Insights showed the new recent-orders query at 81% of load. EXPLAIN showed a backward scan of the created_at index filtering 42 million rows, because nothing indexes customer_id.

parts.label: How
parts.modelAnswer: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY on (customer_id, created_at DESC), which matches the filter and the order and does not lock out checkout's writes; a standard build would have stopped checkout for its duration.

parts.label: Process
parts.modelAnswer: The index was confirmed VALID; new queries on large tables now need an EXPLAIN in review, and index migrations use CONCURRENTLY.

writesLocked.headline: The right index, built the wrong way
writesLocked.body: On a busy table, build indexes with CONCURRENTLY: it takes longer and does not lock out writes. A standard build stops writes until it is done.

campaignSaturated.headline: A missing index, not a small machine
campaignSaturated.body: The plan showed millions of rows filtered to return ten. An index matching the filter and the order fixes it; more CPU does not.

indexed.headline: Good: assessed, then indexed safely
indexed.body: You found the query in Query Insights, read its plan, designed the index for the filter and the order, built it concurrently, confirmed it was valid and fast, and added plan review to releases.

scoring.modelReasoning: Query Insights points to the new recent-orders query, and its plan filters tens of millions of rows to return ten because customer_id has no index. Build an index on (customer_id, created_at DESC), concurrently, because orders takes 300 writes a second and a standard build would lock them out. More CPU needs a restart and barely helps. Check the index is valid, confirm the latency, and add plan review to releases.
